local_facts.title: Hauling someone else's trash takes a district license
local_facts.claim: The Benton County Solid Waste District states that before anyone hauls waste commercially anywhere in Arkansas they must first obtain a license from the local regional solid waste management district, and that the license covers collecting waste from households or businesses on a temporary or permanent basis, transporting it within or through the district, and disposing of it. The district warns that providing collection service without a hauler license violates Arkansas law and district rules. Licensed haulers file an annual application due December 15 and quarterly reports, including reports on loads taken to transfer stations and to the Eco Vista Landfill.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A roll-off box is solid waste collection under that rule, so the company dropping it in your driveway needs a district license. Asking for it before booking separates an established hauler from a truck that will dump the load somewhere it should not go.

local_facts.title: Anything in the street goes through the Street Department
local_facts.claim: The City of Bentonville requires a right-of-way permit at all times during which any work is done upon, in, under, above or about any street, alley, curb, gutter, sidewalk or other public right-of-way in the city. Applications are made online through the city's eTrakit system with a site plan, review takes five business days, a Traffic Management Plan following the MUTCD is required for any closure or detour, and all fees and bonds are paid before the permit issues. The approved permit must be posted where it is visible from the street. The Street Department, at 479-271-3130, administers the permit. The page does not list dumpsters or containers by name.
local_facts.why_it_matters: A box on the driveway or the lot is private property. A box on the street, the curb or the sidewalk is in the right-of-way, so the question goes to the Street Department a week ahead of delivery day, not the morning the truck arrives.

local_facts.title: Fewer permits, bigger houses, a pipeline that doubled
local_facts.claim: Bentonville's 2024 Annual Development Report estimates the city's population at 63,089 on 31 December 2024, up 16 percent from the 54,164 counted in the 2020 Census. The city issued 1,354 building permits in 2024, including 234 residential remodel and addition permits. The average new single-family house permitted grew to 3,115 square feet, up from 2,175 in 2023, and the number of residential units planned rose 92 percent to 2,907.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Bigger houses throw off more framing scrap, drywall and packaging per lot, and nearly three thousand planned units means the job-site dumpster stays a fixture of Bentonville streets. Remodels add a steady second stream of kitchens, baths and floors coming out of existing houses.

local_facts.title: One regional landfill, and separate sites for what it refuses
local_facts.claim: Eco-Vista Landfill in Springdale covers 609 acres, including a 147-acre Class 1 municipal solid waste landfill and a 60-acre Class 4 construction and demolition debris landfill. It does not accept hazardous materials, is open to the public 7 a.m. to 3 p.m. on weekdays, and is closed Saturday and Sunday. The Benton County Solid Waste District runs special waste drop-off sites at 5702 Brookside Road in Centerton and 2307 North Arkansas Street in Rogers for furniture, appliances, electronics, metal items, tires and household hazardous materials, with fees and material limits applying.
local_facts.why_it_matters: Construction debris from a Bentonville box has a permitted place to go, and the weekend closure is why a Friday afternoon swap can wait until Monday. Tires, paint, batteries and refrigerant appliances belong at the district's sites, not under a layer of drywall.
